title: League of Women Voters of Utah v. Utah State Legislature (LWV 1)
description: Whether the district court abused its discretion in refusing to stay its order permanently enjoining the use of H.B. 2004, the 2021 Congressional Map, because the court's ordered remedial process doesn't require compliance with all of Proposition 4.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the Legislative Defendants had other plain, speedy, or adequate remedies available and that the district court's denial of the stay was not an abuse of discretion.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the district court abused its discretion by refusing to stay its injunction on the Congressional Map, contending that the remedial process did not fully comply with Proposition 4 and that no other adequate remedy was available.
decision_outcome: The court denied the Legislative Defendants' petition for extraordinary relief, concluding that they had not demonstrated that the district court abused its discretion in denying the stay of its injunctive order.

title: University of Utah v. Tullis
description: Whether Condemarin v. University Hospital, 775 P.2d 348 (Utah 1989), resolves whether the 2017 GIA's damages cap violates the Utah Constitution, with the plaintiff arguing it does and the defendant arguing it does not.
plaintiff_argument: The Tullises argued that the 2017 GIA's damages cap is unconstitutional as applied to the University, relying on the precedent set by Condemarin v. University Hospital.
defendant_argument: The University argued that Condemarin v. University Hospital is not controlling precedent because it was a plurality decision, the relevant statutes have been repealed and amended, and its legal reasoning is flawed, thus the 2017 GIA's damages cap should apply.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's decision, concluding that Condemarin's holding does not control the applicability of the 2017 GIA's damages cap to the University, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: State v. Labrum
description: Whether the Utah Constitution's Due Process Clause prohibits the State from refiling criminal charges after a magistrate judge has found insufficient evidence at a preliminary hearing.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the magistrate erred in prohibiting refiling under Brickey, that their initial failure to present all theories was an "innocent mistake," and that the Victims' Rights Amendment abrogated the discovery purpose of preliminary hearings, thus allowing refiling.
defendant_argument: Labrum argued that the State's refiling constituted harassment and "hiding the ball" by introducing new theories later, which is prohibited by the Due Process Clause as interpreted by State v. Brickey.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the district court's order dismissing the refiled rape charges and remanded the case for reevaluation under a clarified Brickey standard, allowing the State to potentially proceed with a second preliminary hearing.

title: State v. Rippey
description: Whether subsections (2)(b) and (2)(c) of the Plea Withdrawal Statute (PWS) are constitutional under the Utah Constitution's separation of powers doctrine, with the State arguing they are substantive or jurisdictional and Rippey arguing they are unconstitutional procedural rules.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that subsection (2)(b) of the PWS is substantive or jurisdictional, and therefore a valid exercise of the legislature's authority, and that the PWS does not bar Rippey's challenge to his guilty plea.
defendant_argument: Rippey argued that subsections (2)(b) and (2)(c) of the PWS are unconstitutional because they are procedural rules that violate the separation of powers by infringing on the judiciary's authority to adopt such rules.
decision_outcome: The court held that subsection (2)(b) and the waiver component of subsection (2)(c) of the PWS were unconstitutionally enacted, violating the separation of powers required by the Utah Constitution, and thus do not bar Rippey's challenge to his guilty plea.

title: League of Women Voters of Utah v. Utah State Legislature (LWV 2)
description: Whether Amendment D, proposed by the Utah State Legislature, was properly submitted to voters and published in accordance with the Utah Constitution's requirements, or if procedural failures render it void.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that Amendment D was not properly submitted because its ballot title was misleading and inaccurate, and it was not published in newspapers for two months preceding the election as constitutionally mandated.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the ballot language was sufficient, and they had substantially complied with publication requirements by making the amendment text available online and through news coverage.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's preliminary injunction, declaring Amendment D void and ordering that any votes cast for it not be counted.

title: Jenkins v. Beaver County
description: Whether the statutory postmark requirement for mail-in ballots is constitutional, and whether ballots rejected as untimely due to variations in mail processing should be accepted and counted.
plaintiff_argument: Colby Jenkins argued that the statutory postmark requirement is unconstitutional because it leads to differential treatment of voters based on mail processing location and interferes with the fundamental right to vote by relying on the United States Postal Service.
defendant_argument: The Lieutenant Governor and counties implicitly argued that the statutory postmark requirement is constitutional and that Mr. Jenkins failed to adequately brief his constitutional challenges, thus not demonstrating entitlement to the requested relief.
decision_outcome: The court denied Colby Jenkins's petition for extraordinary relief, upholding the rejection of untimely mail-in ballots.

title: State v. Baugh
description: Whether Brevan Bringhurst Baugh's counsel provided constitutionally ineffective assistance by failing to request more specific unanimity instructions, thereby prejudicing him and invalidating his conviction.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Utah argued that Baugh's counsel's performance was reasonable because Unanimous Verdict Clause caselaw was ambiguous, and that Baugh was not prejudiced by the lack of specific unanimity instructions.
defendant_argument: Brevan Bringhurst Baugh argued that his counsel rendered constitutionally ineffective assistance by failing to request jury instructions that would have properly instructed the jury on its constitutional duty to be unanimous as to each element of each convicted count.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, vacating Brevan Bringhurst Baugh's conviction for aggravated sexual abuse of a child.

title: Sports Medicine Research & Testing Lab. v. Board of Equalization of Salt Lake County
description: Whether Sports Medicine Research and Testing Laboratory's property is used exclusively for charitable purposes, thus qualifying for a property tax exemption under the Utah Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Sports Medicine argued its property is used for charitable purposes, citing discounted testing for government/charitable organizations, that market-rate testing for professional athletes is necessary to sustain its philanthropic mission and generate data, and that vacant space is for future charitable expansion.
defendant_argument: The Board of Equalization and Tax Commission argued that Sports Medicine's market-rate testing for professional sports leagues generates significant profit and therefore the property is not used exclusively for charitable purposes.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Tax Commission's denial of Sports Medicine's request for a property tax exemption, ruling that the property was not used exclusively for charitable purposes.

title: Bingham v. Gourley
description: Whether the Utah Health Care Malpractice Act's four-year statute of repose is unconstitutional under the Utah Constitution's Open Courts Clause, Uniform Operation of Laws Provision, and the federal Equal Protection Clause.
plaintiff_argument: The statute of repose is unconstitutional because it violates the Open Courts Clause, Uniform Operation of Laws Provision, and the Equal Protection Clause by denying individuals with difficult-to-detect injuries the right to seek redress.
defendant_argument: The statute of repose is constitutional and does not violate any of the mentioned provisions, serving a legitimate legislative purpose to address a health care crisis.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's dismissal of Bingham's claim, rejecting her constitutional challenge to the Utah Health Care Malpractice Act's four-year statute of repose.

title: Salt Lake County v. Utah State Tax Commission
description: Whether the Aircraft Valuation Law, as applied to Delta Air Lines' aircraft, resulted in an assessment below fair market value in violation of the Utah Constitution, and whether the Aircraft Valuation Law is unconstitutional on its face for divesting the Commission of its power to assess airline property.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Salt Lake County, argued that the Aircraft Valuation Law, as applied, resulted in an assessment below fair market value, violating the Utah Constitution's requirement for uniform property assessment, and that the law is facially unconstitutional because it strips the Tax Commission of its original assessment authority over airline property.
defendant_argument: The defendants, Utah State Tax Commission and Delta Air Lines, Inc., argued that the Aircraft Valuation Law was correctly applied, that the County failed to provide sufficient evidence to trigger an alternative valuation method, and that the law is constitutional both as applied and on its face.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Utah State Tax Commission's decision, ruling that the Aircraft Valuation Law is constitutional both as applied to Delta's 2017 assessment and on its face.

title: Kell v. State
description: Whether the district court erred in dismissing Troy Michael Kell's second petition for post-conviction relief based on time and procedural bars, or if applying these bars violates his constitutional rights.
plaintiff_argument: Kell argued that the PCRA's time and procedural bars should not apply because his delay was due to ineffective assistance of counsel and that their application violates his constitutional rights under the Suspension, Due Process, and Open Courts Clauses.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the district court correctly dismissed Kell's petition because his five-and-a-half-year delay in filing after discovering new evidence means his arguments do not overcome the PCRA's time and procedural limitations.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's grant of summary judgment and dismissal of Kell's second petition for post-conviction relief.

title: State v. Barnett
description: Whether the Utah Constitution's Bail Provision prohibits judges from granting bail to defendants charged with a felony while on probation, or merely removes the guarantee of bail while still allowing judicial discretion.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that article I, section 8(1) of the Utah Constitution mandates that a judge deny bail to a defendant charged with a felony if that defendant is already serving probation on a felony conviction.
defendant_argument: Barnett argued that the phrase "shall be bailable except" means that while a person charged with a felony on probation is not guaranteed bail, a district court still retains discretion to grant it.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the district court's decision, ruling that the Bail Provision's plain language and historical understanding support the interpretation that judges retain discretion to grant bail even in cases where bail is not constitutionally guaranteed.

title: Lord v. Salt Lake County Clerk
description: Whether a property tax increase approved by a school district is subject to a referendum, with petitioners arguing it is and respondents arguing it is not.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that a school district's property tax increase is subject to a referendum under the Utah Constitution and relevant statutes, despite conceding statutory definitions were not perfectly aligned.
defendant_argument: The respondents argued that school districts are not subject to referenda under the Utah Constitution or relevant statutes, citing intentional omission of school districts from referendum provisions and statutory limitations to counties, cities, and towns.
decision_outcome: The court denied the petitioners' request for extraordinary relief, ruling that they failed to demonstrate that a school district's tax increase is subject to a referendum.

title: State v. Soto
description: Whether improper communications by court personnel to jurors, suggesting the defendant's guilt, trigger a rebuttable presumption of prejudice against the defendant.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the improper contacts did not trigger a presumption of prejudice, or if they did, the trial court's actions (juror interviews and curative instruction) had already rebutted it by proving harmlessness.
defendant_argument: Soto argued that the improper communications by court personnel to the jury violated his constitutional right to an impartial jury and triggered a rebuttable presumption of prejudice.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the court of appeals' decision, ruling that Soto was entitled to a rebuttable presumption of prejudice and remanded the case to the district court to determine if the State can rebut this presumption beyond a reasonable doubt.

title: Salt Lake City Corp. v. Utah Inland Port Authority
description: Whether the Utah Inland Port Authority Act's zoning provisions violate the Uniform Operation of Laws Clause and Ripper Clause of the Utah Constitution, and whether its tax provisions also violate these clauses.
plaintiff_argument: Salt Lake City argued the Act's zoning and tax provisions violate the Uniform Operation of Laws Clause by treating specific cities disparately and the Ripper Clause by delegating municipal functions and interfering with municipal money.
defendant_argument: The Utah Inland Port Authority and the State argued the Act's provisions are constitutional, as they are rationally related to a legitimate legislative purpose and are direct legislative mandates, not improper delegations of municipal power.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the dismissal of Salt Lake City's challenges to the zoning provisions of the Utah Inland Port Authority Act, finding them constitutional, but declined to rule on the tax provisions, deeming those claims potentially moot due to recent amendments.

title: Laws v. Grayeyes
description: Whether Kelly Laws had standing to challenge Willie Grayeyes's election as county commissioner due to an alleged lack of residency, and whether Grayeyes was entitled to attorney fees.
plaintiff_argument: Laws argued that Willie Grayeyes was not a resident of San Juan County and therefore ineligible to serve as county commissioner, and that Laws had standing to challenge the election either statutorily or traditionally.
defendant_argument: Grayeyes argued he was a resident of San Juan County and eligible to serve, and that Kelly Laws lacked standing to challenge his election. He also sought attorney fees, claiming Laws's challenge was in bad faith or that he was entitled to fees under the private attorney general doctrine.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court dismissed Kelly Laws's challenge to Willie Grayeyes's election for lack of standing, concluding Laws had not alleged a sufficiently particularized injury. The court also affirmed the district court's denial of attorney fees to Grayeyes.

title: Patterson v. State
description: Whether the Post-Conviction Remedies Act's (PCRA) time limitations should be tolled or are unconstitutional if they constrain the court's Constitutional writ authority, and whether an 'egregious injustice' exception applies to procedural time bars.
plaintiff_argument: Patterson argued that the PCRA's time limitations should be tolled due to ineffective assistance of counsel or newly discovered evidence, or that the court's Constitutional writ power exists independently of the PCRA, rendering the PCRA unconstitutional if it limits this power.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Patterson's petition was time-barred under the PCRA, that the PCRA wholly regulates the court's writ authority, and that no statutory or equitable tolling or 'egregious injustice' exception applied to save his claims.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's dismissal of Patterson's petition as time-barred under the PCRA, but remanded two claims based on newly discovered evidence for further consideration.

title: In re Childers-Gray
description: Whether Utah courts have the jurisdiction and authority to adjudicate petitions for legal sex designation changes, and what legal standard should apply to such petitions.
plaintiff_argument: Appellants argued they have a common-law right to change their legal sex designation to reflect their gender identity, supported by medical evidence, and that the district court erred in denying their petitions.
defendant_argument: The district court (implicitly representing the State's position) argued that there is no statutory or common-law framework for courts to adjudicate sex-change petitions, making it a legislative matter and a nonjusticiable political question.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's denial, holding that Utah courts have jurisdiction and common-law authority to adjudicate sex-change petitions, and established a two-prong test for approval, remanding with instructions to grant the petitions.

title: Feldman v. Salt Lake City Corp.
description: Whether the Limitations on Landowner Liability Act bars wrongful death claims, violates the Utah Constitution, and whether Ms. Feldman's death was caused by an inherent risk under the Act.
plaintiff_argument: The Act does not bar wrongful death claims, or if it does, it violates the Utah Constitution, and Ms. Feldman's death was not caused by an inherent risk of recreating in the Park.
defendant_argument: The Act bars wrongful death claims, does not violate the Utah Constitution, and Ms. Feldman's death was caused by an inherent risk of entering the creek.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the district court's dismissal and remanded the case for further proceedings, finding that while the Act can bar wrongful death claims and is constitutional, the plaintiffs sufficiently alleged that the death was not caused by an inherent risk.
